newsitem.title: USA: Hancock sales practices under scrutiny by states.
newsitem.headline: Hancock sales practices under scrutiny by states.

text.p: John Hancock Mutual Life Insurance Co on Friday said it was in talks with the Massachusetts Division of Insurance and regulators from other states about allegations of deceptive sales practices.

"The allegations and time period are exactly the same as those spelled out in a class-action suit filed against us in 1995," the company said in a short statement. "We've been talking about them with the (insurance) commissioner's office and regulators from a number of other states for many months now, and we will continue to do so until this is resolved."
A spokesman for Hancock, contacted by Reuters, did not identify the other states in talks with the company.
Hancock faces a class-action lawsuit charging that the company improperly "churned" policies to generate fresh commissions for agents and revenues for the company.

The Massachusetts Division of Insurance said it recently began a broad investigation into Hancock's sales practices and was seeking company documents on disciplinary actions against its agents over the past 18 years.

Michael Goetz, a spokesman for the state insurance division, said the investigation was in the early stages and covered a deceptive sales practice known as churning -- marketing life insurance as an investment and policies that include so-called vanishing premiums.

"We've made a very substantial request of them to provide us all of the names of agents they have disciplined," he said. The agency has also requested sales marketing literature and procedural manuals to train agents.

"The purpose of that is so that we can go through it and see whether it bears out allegations of unfair conduct," he said. "They've indicated a willingness to cooperate with our investigation," he said.

The investigation into John Hancock is just the latest shadow cast over the insurance industry. The Prudential Insurance Co of America could end up paying more than $2.5 billion to policyholders to settle class-action lawsuits alleging that the company engaged in deceptive sales practices.
